An `image` is optional: `src` is a path under media/updates/, `alt` describes it for anyone who cannot see it, `focus` is a CSS object-position keeping the important part in frame when the card crops it, and `credit` names whoever the photograph belongs to. updates.title: We've asked West Sussex for its bus planning records
updates.author: Connor R
updates.summary: A Freedom of Information request asks West Sussex County Council where its bus money goes, what it has discussed with Brighton & Hove, and who uses the Discovery ticket. The council has until 9 October to reply.

image.alt: An open copy of the Freedom of Information Act 2000, with the royal coat of arms above the title and the opening words of the Act below it.
image.credit_note: The site owner reports this photograph is under a public licence. The photographer, the licence and a source link are not recorded yet; put them in `credit` once known. Not guessed here.

updates.body:
On 13 September we sent West Sussex County Council a Freedom of Information request about buses across the boundary between Adur and Brighton & Hove. The council acknowledged it the same day as reference FOI/13765. The Act gives it 20 working days to answer, which runs to 9 October.

Most of what this site says about the gap either side of Portslade comes from the published timetable: how many buses are scheduled, where they stop, which tickets cover them. That shows what the network looks like. It can't show why. A timetable doesn't record how the council spends its bus funding, or whether anyone has sat down with Brighton & Hove to plan a route that crosses the line.

So we asked for four things.

Where the money goes. Bus Service Improvement Plan and Local Authority Bus Grant funding since April 2022, broken down across the seven districts and boroughs of West Sussex, and the subsidy paid each year to supported services on the A259 coast road or on routes that cross into Brighton & Hove. If Adur gets less than its neighbours, that should show up here.

Any plans to run buses across the boundary, at whatever stage they reached: proposed, under review, rejected or planned. That includes anything an operator has put forward about running further west than Shoreham, or further east into Brighton.

Minutes and agendas from the Enhanced Partnership board and forum since January 2023, wherever cross-boundary travel, the coastal corridor or working with Brighton & Hove came up. The Enhanced Partnership is where the council and the operators agree how local buses run. If a joined-up plan with Brighton & Hove were being discussed anywhere, it would be there.

How many Discovery tickets are sold on West Sussex services, and whether the council knows how many people use them to get to work rather than for days out. It is the only ticket every operator on this coast accepts, but it is priced and sold as a leisure rover. We want to know whether anyone is tracking who ends up relying on it.

We don't know yet what will come back. Some of this may not be held in the form we asked for, and a request can be cut down if answering it would cost more than the Act allows. We asked the council to tell us how to narrow it if that happens, rather than refuse it outright.

The request and every reply to it are public on WhatDoTheyKnow, so you can read the council's answer as soon as it lands. We'll write up what it says here, and the boundary evidence on the Route view shows the timetable figures it will be read against.

links.label: The request and the council's replies (WhatDoTheyKnow)

updates.title: Single fares drop to £2 in January
updates.summary: The national cap on a single bus fare falls from £3 to £2 from 1 January 2027.

image.alt: The destination display on the front of a double-decker bus reading “£2 Fare Cap”.
image.credit_note: Source and permission not recorded. Needs the site owner to confirm where this came from and on what terms, or to be replaced. Not invented here: an attribution that is guessed is worse than one that is missing.

updates.body:
It matters more here than the headline suggests. Crossing the Worthing/Brighton DayRider boundary does not by itself require two buses, because the 700 runs straight through it. But a ticket boundary is where the day-ticket options stop covering you, so the fare cap is what keeps that journey at £6 return today and £4 from January. That is cheaper than every day ticket covering the same trip, which tells you something about how those zones are drawn.

Where two buses are needed, Lancing to Brighton say, it is two singles each way: £12 return today, £8 once the cap drops.

The Ticket view journey checker prices singles alongside day tickets, so you can see which is cheaper for a given trip.

updates.title: Stagecoach moves to Ticketer, the same system B&H already runs
updates.summary: From September both major operators on this coast will run the same ticketing platform. That weakens the technical objection to accepting each other's tickets; it does not settle the commercial one.

image.alt: A contactless bank card held against a blue Ticketer reader on a bus, the driver’s console display above it reading “Ticketer smart ticketing”.
image.credit_note: Source and permission not recorded. Needs the site owner to confirm where this came from and on what terms, or to be replaced. Not invented here: an attribution that is guessed is worse than one that is missing.

updates.body:
Stagecoach has appointed Ticketer as its supplier of ticketing and real-time information technology, deploying the detachable TK300 ticket machine across its fleet. The national rollout begins in September. The platform combines electronic ticketing, vehicle location and real-time information in one system.

Every Brighton & Hove bus already runs Ticketer. So from September, the two operators that meet at Shoreham, where Brighton & Hove's network ends and Stagecoach's carries on west, will be issuing and reading tickets on the same equipment from the same supplier.

What this changes is the strength of one argument, not the state of the network. Mutual ticket acceptance has always carried a technical objection: two different ticketing systems, two sets of hardware. A shared supplier makes that objection harder to sustain.

It does not by itself make acceptance possible. A rollout beginning in September is not the same as local completion, and common equipment is not the same as interoperable products or an agreed way of splitting the revenue between operators. Those are commercial decisions, and nobody has announced them. We are asking for them; we are not reporting them as done.

links.label: Stagecoach selects Ticketer for nationwide ticketing (routeone)
